records.problem: I need to see the public address this connection presents to the internet, and tell IPv4 from IPv6, without an app or an account.
solutionWeaknesses: Google answers the number and stops, so IPv4 versus IPv6 and CGNAT go unexplained
the big lookup sites wrap the number in ads, trackers, and a map
several copy the wrong family because v4 and v6 are stacked without labels
userFailures: Copies the IPv6 address into a form that only accepts IPv4 and thinks the lookup is wrong
Reads a 100.64 CGNAT address as their public IP and opens a firewall hole that nothing can reach
Leaves a VPN on, copies that egress, and wonders why a home whitelist still fails
Sees only one family on a dual-stack path and assumes the other does not exist

records.problem: I have an IPv4 address and a prefix or mask and I need the network, broadcast, usable range, and wildcard without doing the bit math by hand.
solutionWeaknesses: most still default to classful masks when you paste a host address
ad-supported pages bury the usable range below a table of every prefix
/31 and /32 are shown with the same minus-two host rule that does not apply
userFailures: Pastes 192.168.1.50/24 and treats that host as the network in a firewall rule
Uses total minus two on a /31 point-to-point link and thinks the subnet is empty
Enters a dotted mask with a hole in the bits and accepts a silently rounded prefix
Copies the broadcast as a usable host into a cloud security group

records.problem: I need to turn a dotted IPv4 address into its 32-bit decimal, hex, or binary form, and back, without a spreadsheet formula.
solutionWeaknesses: converters that take a generic integer do not reject 256 in an octet
hex output often drops the leading zeros that packet captures show
userFailures: Treats the four octets as a base-10 number like 19216811 and gets a different host
Pastes an IPv6 address into an IPv4 converter and reads the truncation as a result
